Pregnancy

Cupping during pregnancy: evidence, risks and safer next steps

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Cupping is often promoted for pain, circulation or pregnancy wellbeing. Those claims need careful examination. No pregnancy stage has been established as a safe window, and the symptom prompting treatment deserves an appropriate maternity assessment.

Dry and wet cupping are different procedures

Cupping is used in traditional medicine in several parts of the world. Cups create suction against the skin, sometimes using heat and sometimes a mechanical pump. Dry cupping leaves the skin unpierced. Wet cupping, sometimes called hijama, adds small cuts or punctures so blood is drawn into the cup.

This distinction matters because wet cupping adds deliberate blood loss and an open wound. Dry cupping can still cause bruising, burns or skin injury. A long history of use or availability in a clinic does not establish that either procedure is suitable during pregnancy.

A local skin effect does not prove a pregnancy benefit

Suction changes the skin and small blood vessels in the treated area. People may describe warmth, loosened muscles or temporary pain relief. These experiences do not show that the procedure improves the placenta, speeds tissue healing throughout the body or produces better pregnancy outcomes.

Research into cupping is generally limited and often of low quality. Some studies suggest possible pain relief, but the evidence is not strong enough to support the wide range of advertised benefits. Results from non-pregnant adults also cannot establish safety for a pregnant person or fetus.

When a practitioner makes a claim, ask which outcome was measured and whether pregnant participants were actually studied. A change in local circulation is not the same as a demonstrated reduction in complications.

There is no established safe pregnancy window

Cupping is not a proven antenatal treatment. Because its effects during pregnancy are insufficiently studied and the procedure has known risks, it is best avoided during pregnancy. Discuss the symptom you want to treat with your midwife or obstetric clinician so an appropriate alternative can be considered.

There is no reliable basis for calling months four to six the best or safest time for cupping. Avoiding the upper or lower abdomen does not establish that treatment elsewhere is safe. Similarly, a provider’s experience cannot replace evidence about pregnancy outcomes.

An explanation that suction simply diverts the fetus’s blood supply into the parent’s skin is not an established account of what happens. The practical concern is uncertainty combined with possible skin injury, infection, fainting and, with wet cupping, blood loss. Advice should focus on those concerns rather than speculative mechanisms.

Health conditions can add to the risk

Anaemia, a bleeding disorder such as haemophilia, medicines that affect clotting, dehydration or a tendency to faint make unnecessary blood loss particularly concerning. Fever, active infection, damaged skin and some inflammatory skin conditions also need attention rather than another procedure.

Cupping over varicose veins or other vulnerable vessels should not be treated as a harmless home practice. People with significant heart disease, a recent serious cardiac event, suspected cancer or another unexplained illness need medical assessment of that problem.

Lists that use a fixed six-month interval after cardiac arrest or describe menstruation as the only time to avoid treatment should not be read as a validated safety rule. Being outside a listed category does not prove safety, and pregnancy itself remains a reason to avoid cupping rather than try to find an exception.

Detox and fertility claims are not established

Cupping before conception is sometimes promoted as a way to remove toxins, strengthen immunity, improve metabolism or make ovulation easier. There is no established evidence that drawing blood this way prepares the body for pregnancy or improves the chance of a healthy birth.

Stress, anxiety, depression and pain deserve support in their own right. Feeling relaxed after a treatment does not prove that it corrects infertility, and difficulty conceiving should not be blamed on failing to relax. Ask for assessment and suitable mental-health or pain support when these concerns affect daily life.

Preconception care should address actual needs such as medicine review, nutrition, recommended folic acid and management of existing conditions. Do not replace that care with a package promising a fertility detox. If you could already be pregnant, mention that before considering any elective procedure.

High blood pressure needs maternity care

High blood pressure during pregnancy can affect both the pregnant person and the baby. It needs monitoring and, when indicated, prescribed treatment. Although some medicines require a change in pregnancy, pregnancy-appropriate options exist; cupping is not an established substitute.

Do not stop a blood-pressure prescription because a practitioner says medicines are unsafe. Ask the prescribing clinician to review the specific medicine and explain the plan for blood pressure, urine checks and fetal monitoring.

A severe headache, visual disturbance, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling or feeling very unwell can be warning signs of pre-eclampsia. Contact maternity services promptly rather than booking a treatment for headache or muscle tension and waiting to see whether it helps.

Cupping does not prevent miscarriage

Early pregnancy loss is often related to a problem with the embryo’s chromosomes. It is not generally caused by the pregnant person’s blood being too thick, and it is not evidence that they failed to cleanse or balance their body.

Some specific conditions, including antiphospholipid syndrome, can increase pregnancy complications. These require proper testing and an individual medical plan, sometimes involving prescribed low-dose aspirin and heparin. Removing blood through cupping does not treat the underlying condition or replace those medicines.

If you have experienced a loss, ask what evaluation is appropriate for your history. No complementary procedure can promise to prevent another miscarriage. If bleeding or pain occurs in a current pregnancy, seek maternity advice rather than attempting to treat the presumed cause yourself.

Fetal growth and clot-prevention claims are unsupported

The placenta transfers oxygen and nutrients between the parent and fetus. That does not mean that taking blood from the skin improves the quality of blood reaching the placenta. There is no established evidence that cupping increases fetal height, improves nutrition to the fetus or corrects a growth problem.

Growth concerns are assessed through the pregnancy history, examination and appropriate scans or monitoring. If the team recommends follow-up, keep those appointments rather than relying on a treatment advertised to improve circulation.

Claims that cupping prevents clots or improves cardiovascular function during pregnancy are also not established. Headaches and body pain may have many causes; the first step is to identify the cause and choose care suitable for pregnancy, not assume a circulation treatment addresses all of them.

It does not prevent newborn jaundice

Newborn jaundice involves a build-up of bilirubin, a yellow pigment produced as red blood cells are broken down. A newborn liver may not yet process it efficiently. Some babies also have other causes, including blood-group incompatibility, infection or liver disease.

There is no evidence that cupping during pregnancy prevents this process. After birth, a baby with jaundice needs assessment based on age, bilirubin level, feeding and general health. Cupping is not a substitute for these checks or for treatment when required.

It is also too broad to say that nothing done in pregnancy can reduce any jaundice risk. Antenatal blood-group and antibody care, including anti-D when indicated, can help prevent particular forms of haemolytic disease. That is a specific medical intervention, not proof for cupping or a guarantee against ordinary newborn jaundice.

Blood loss and infection are meaningful risks

Wet cupping removes blood. Repeated or substantial loss may contribute to iron deficiency or anaemia, which can cause fatigue, weakness, dizziness or shortness of breath. Severe bleeding or collapse needs urgent medical attention. Low blood pressure or existing anaemia makes these concerns more relevant.

Both forms can leave marks; burns, scarring, persistent discolouration and skin infection can occur. Equipment exposed to blood can transmit infection if it is inadequately sterilised or reused. NCCIH specifically warns about hepatitis B and C; any suspected exposure to another person’s blood needs prompt medical advice.

Single-use equipment and hygiene do not remove every risk or establish pregnancy safety. Conversely, an isolated report of a complication does not tell us how often it occurs. Claims that cupping routinely causes clots, like claims that it prevents them, should not be made without adequate evidence.

If you have already had cupping

Having undergone a session does not mean that you or your baby have necessarily been harmed. Tell your maternity clinician when it occurred, whether the skin was cut, where it was performed, whether there was bleeding and whether you have any symptoms. This allows advice based on the actual exposure.

Seek prompt care for a burn, worsening pain, spreading redness, pus or fever. If equipment may have been shared or contaminated, report this promptly because assessment after a blood exposure can be time-sensitive. Do not wait for an infection to become visible.

Uncontrolled bleeding, fainting or severe weakness needs urgent or emergency help. Pregnancy bleeding, significant abdominal pain, concerning headache or reduced fetal movements once you have an established pattern should be discussed with maternity services immediately. These symptoms need assessment regardless of whether cupping caused them.

Choose care for the problem you actually have

Bring the reason you were considering cupping to your pregnancy-care team: headache, back discomfort, anxiety, a blood-pressure concern or fear about the baby’s growth. Each has a different assessment and different useful options.

For example, a musculoskeletal problem may benefit from pregnancy-appropriate movement advice or physiotherapy, while anaemia requires investigation and treatment of its cause. Persistent anxiety may call for practical and psychological support. A clinician can also advise which medicines are suitable for your circumstances.

Ask what benefit is expected, what risks are known and when to seek further help. A reassuring plan should address your symptom and concerns directly without promising that one procedure can prevent miscarriage, jaundice and growth problems at the same time.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Research does not establish cupping as a safe or effective pregnancy treatment.

Claims about fertility, miscarriage prevention, fetal growth and newborn jaundice are unsupported.

Wet cupping adds blood-loss and wound risks; dry cupping also has potential harms.

How BeMama can help

Tell your pregnancy-care team what you hope to treat and ask for a plan that addresses that specific problem. If you have already had cupping, describe the exposure without assuming harm.

When to seek help

Seek urgent help for uncontrolled bleeding, collapse, fever or a suspected blood exposure. Contact maternity services promptly for pregnancy bleeding, severe headache, significant abdominal pain or reduced fetal movements.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Avoid cupping during pregnancy because safety is insufficiently established.
  • Months four to six are not a proven safe window.
  • Do not replace blood-pressure or clotting treatment with bloodletting.
  • Cupping cannot be relied on to prevent miscarriage or jaundice.
  • After a session, report symptoms and exposure details to your clinician.

Frequently asked questions

Is dry cupping safer than wet cupping in pregnancy?

Dry cupping avoids deliberate blood removal, but it can still injure the skin and its pregnancy safety is not established. The distinction does not make it a recommended pregnancy treatment.

Are months four to six a safe time for cupping?

No reliable evidence establishes months four to six as a safe window. Avoiding the abdomen or choosing an experienced practitioner does not resolve the uncertainty.

Can cupping detox my body before conception?

There is no established evidence that it removes toxins in a way that improves ovulation, conception or healthy birth. Preconception care should address actual nutrition, medicine and health needs.

Can it replace blood-pressure medicine?

No. High blood pressure in pregnancy needs monitoring and appropriate prescribed treatment. Do not stop a medicine without the prescribing clinician’s advice.

Does thick blood cause most miscarriages?

No. Many early losses involve chromosomal problems. Specific clotting-related conditions need diagnosis and medical treatment; they do not justify cupping as miscarriage prevention.

Will cupping help the baby grow taller?

There is no established evidence for that claim. A concern about fetal growth requires maternity assessment and appropriate monitoring.

Can it prevent jaundice after birth?

No evidence supports this. Babies need the usual jaundice checks, and some need bilirubin testing or treatment. Antenatal anti-D care for a specific blood-group risk is a separate medical intervention.

Does sterile equipment make it safe?

Sterility reduces some infection risks but does not remove blood loss, fainting, burns or uncertainty about pregnancy outcomes. It is not a safety guarantee.

I already had a session. Should I assume the baby is harmed?

No. Tell your maternity clinician what happened and report symptoms or possible blood exposure. An individual assessment is more useful than assuming a complication occurred.

Which symptoms after cupping need help?

Promptly report fever, spreading redness, pus, burns or suspected contaminated equipment. Uncontrolled bleeding or collapse needs emergency help, and concerning pregnancy symptoms need immediate maternity advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
